passage:
In the London flat, Kaito crouched by the door. “Amara, where's your other shoe?”
Amara looked at him. Nothing. She looked at the ceiling.
“She's ignoring you,” said Grandma from the kitchen.
Kaito opened his mouth to ask again, then closed it. He counted slowly in his head, one, two, three, four, five.
Amara frowned, turned, and pointed under the sofa. “Dere!”
“There it is,” said Kaito. “Thank you."

qa.q: Where was Amara's other shoe?
qa.a: Under the sofa, where Amara pointed.

qa.q: What was Amara likely feeling and doing during her long pause?
qa.a: She was most likely thinking hard about where the shoe was, not ignoring Kaito; her frown before pointing suggests effort, perhaps a little confusion.

qa.q: What small step helped Amara answer?
qa.a: Kaito waited a few seconds instead of repeating the question, which gave her time to work it out.

qa.q: How did Grandma read Amara's silence?
qa.a: Grandma read it as Amara ignoring Kaito.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler taking a long time to answer because she is processing, and an adult waiting a few seconds to give her room.

passage:
At dinner in the Lucknow flat, Usha's brother was telling Sarita about his school trip.
“And then the bus—”
“DOGGY! Doggy, doggy!” Usha shouted over him, banging her spoon.
“Usha!” said her brother. “So rude!”
“She's little, she hasn't learned turns yet,” said Sarita. She held up a hand to Usha. “Bhaiya's turn. Then Usha's turn.”
Her brother finished. Sarita turned. “Now Usha's turn.”
Usha beamed. “Doggy!"

qa.q: What was Usha's brother telling Sarita about?
qa.a: He was telling Sarita about his school trip.

qa.q: Why did Usha shout over her brother, and what was she feeling?
qa.a: She was excited about the dog and eager to share it; she has not yet learned turn-taking, so it was not rudeness.

qa.q: How did Sarita help Usha learn to take turns?
qa.a: Sarita gave a short, clear rule, "Bhaiya's turn. Then Usha's turn," and then kept the promise by giving Usha her turn.

qa.q: How did Usha's brother feel when she shouted over him?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and interrupted, calling her rude.

grounding: It shows a toddler talking over others because turn-taking is not yet formed, and an adult modelling your turn, my turn.

passage:
Monday. Neelam's parents were away for the night. Nikita Masi played a lullaby on a small speaker. Neelam kept fussing, twisting in the cot.
Tuesday. Nikita picked her up, held her close, swayed slowly and sang the same lullaby herself, off-key and soft. Neelam's head grew heavy on her shoulder.
Thursday. Nikita forgot the words, so she hummed a made-up tune at the same slow pace. Neelam was asleep within minutes.

qa.q: What did Nikita do when she forgot the words on Thursday?
qa.a: She hummed a made-up tune at the same slow pace.

qa.q: Why did Neelam settle on Tuesday but not on Monday?
qa.a: On Tuesday she felt safe and comforted in Nikita's arms, with her warm voice and slow swaying; the lullaby from the speaker alone didn't give her that closeness.

qa.q: What could Nikita keep doing on nights when Neelam is unsettled?
qa.a: Hold her close and sing or hum slowly in her own voice, since the closeness and rhythm matter more than the right tune or words.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel when a made-up tune works just as well?
qa.a: Nikita would likely feel relieved and more confident about caring for Neelam while her parents are away.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler settling to a caregiver's lullaby because of the slow rhythm, warm voice and closeness rather than the tune.

passage:
On the veranda of the farmhouse, Uma Aaji sat sorting beans. Arohi sat beside her with a bowl of her own, dropping beans in one by one.
“Mmm-mmm-maaa,” Arohi hummed, a wandering tune, swaying.
Uma smiled and hummed it back. “Mmm-mmm-maaa.”
Arohi stopped, looked at her, and cooed, “Ooo!” Then she hummed again, a little louder, waiting for the echo.

qa.q: What was Uma Aaji sorting on the veranda?
qa.a: She was sorting beans.

qa.q: What does Arohi's humming and swaying suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she was content and relaxed, settled into play beside her Aaji.

qa.q: Which choice by Uma built a connection, and why?
qa.a: Humming Arohi's tune back to her, which turned the humming into a shared back-and-forth and practises the rhythm of conversation.

qa.q: What is it like for Uma when Arohi waits for the echo?
qa.a: Uma probably feels touched and amused that Arohi has made it into a game they share.

grounding: It shows a toddler humming and cooing wordless tunes while playing contentedly, and an adult echoing the tune.

passage:
Outside the anganwadi in the kasba, Saurabh clung to his Maa's sari.
She knelt. “Two kisses. One wave at the window. After khichdi, Maa comes.” Kiss, kiss.
Saurabh cried and held on. Then he let Farhan, the helper, lift him. He waved. Then cried again.
Last month she used to slip away while he played, and he screamed for an hour.
Now, at the window, Saurabh waved once more. His crying slowed to hiccups.

qa.q: When does Maa say she will come back?
qa.a: After khichdi, Maa comes.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling as he cried, clung and waved in turns?
qa.a: He was sad and anxious about Maa leaving, while also starting to accept the goodbye, so his feelings were mixed.

qa.q: Why does the short goodbye routine work better than slipping away?
qa.a: It is predictable and tells Saurabh what will happen, so he can manage his distress; sneaking away left him screaming for an hour.

qa.q: How might Maa feel doing the goodbye while Saurabh cries?
qa.a: She probably feels sad and torn, but reassured when his crying slows at the window.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler at drop-off crying, clinging and waving in turns, and a short predictable farewell ritual helping more than sneaking away.

passage:
I'm Kunal, from upstairs. Most mornings little Madhuri waves bye-bye to the milkman, and when she sees me on the stairs she babbles, “Aa-lo!” and flaps her hand.
Last Sunday my friend came with me. Madhuri took one look at him and hid behind her mother's dupatta.
“Say hello, Madhuri,” my friend said.
Her mother just smiled. “She's shy today. No need.” Madhuri peeped out at me and gave a tiny wave.

qa.q: Who does Madhuri wave bye-bye to most mornings?
qa.a: She waves bye-bye to the milkman.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when she hid behind her mother's dupatta?
qa.a: She was shy and unsure of the new person, while still feeling friendly towards Kunal, whom she knew.

qa.q: Why was her mother right not to force a hello?
qa.a: Forcing a greeting on a shy toddler can add to her unease; letting her choose meant she still gave a tiny wave.

qa.q: How might Kunal's friend have felt when Madhuri hid?
qa.a: The friend may have felt a little disappointed or awkward, expecting a hello.

grounding: It shows a toddler waving and babbling hello to people she knows and hiding when shy, with an adult not forcing a greeting.

passage:
At the playschool in Indiranagar, Gautam Sir had been away sick all week.
On Monday he walked in, and Yusuf, sitting with the blocks, froze. Then his whole face lit up. He dropped the blocks, stretched out his arms and toddled across the room as fast as his legs would go, squealing.
Gautam crouched and caught him. “Yusuf! I told you I'd come back!”
Yusuf patted his cheek, grinning.

qa.q: How long had Gautam Sir been away sick?
qa.a: He had been away sick all week.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when his face lit up and he toddled over?
qa.a: He was overjoyed to see a caregiver he trusts come back, shown by his squeals, reaching arms and grin.

qa.q: What does Gautam's reminder "I told you I'd come back" show about good goodbyes?
qa.a: Telling a child you will return, and then doing so, makes goodbyes and reunions predictable and strengthens the child's trust.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel when Yusuf runs to him?
qa.a: He would probably feel touched and welcomed back after a week away.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler lighting up, reaching and toddling towards a returning caregiver, a sign of secure attachment and joy.

passage:
“Bus!” Trisha pointed from the pram.
“Yes, a big red bus!” said Dolma.
“Dog!”
“A sleepy dog, under the cart.”
“Moon!”
Dolma looked up. “You're right, there's the moon, in the daytime!”
“She's been chattering nonstop,” said Grandpa, walking beside them.
“I love it,” said Dolma. “She's telling us what she sees.”
Trisha pointed again. “Ba-loon!”
“Blue balloon,” said Dolma, grinning.

qa.q: Where was the dog?
qa.a: The sleepy dog was under the cart.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling as she kept pointing and naming things?
qa.a: She was excited and eager to share what caught her interest, and Dolma's answers kept her going.

qa.q: What does Dolma do that helps Trisha's vocabulary?
qa.a: She names each thing back with a little more detail, like "a big red bus" and "blue balloon."

qa.q: How does Grandpa see Trisha's pointing and naming?
qa.a: Grandpa sees it as nonstop chattering, a bit much, while Dolma enjoys it.

grounding: It shows a toddler pointing and naming objects to share attention, and an adult naming back to build her vocabulary.

passage:
Preschool note, Tuesday. From Swati.
Yamini's favourite question this week is “Wha-dat?” with her voice going up at the end and a pointing finger.
She asked about the fan five times this morning. She knows the word “fan.” But each time she looked at my face, not the fan.
I answered each time, “Fan!”, with a smile, and she grinned back and moved on.
I think the question is partly just her way of saying “talk to me."

qa.q: How many times did Yamini ask about the fan this morning?
qa.a: She asked about the fan five times.

qa.q: What did Yamini want when she asked "Wha-dat?" about a fan she already knew?
qa.a: She wanted Swati's attention and a friendly exchange; looking at Swati's face rather than the fan suggests she was enjoying the connection more than needing the word.

qa.q: Was Swati's response enough, and why?
qa.a: Yes, a quick answer and a smile met both the question and Yamini's wish for attention, so she was happy and moved on.

qa.q: What would change if Swati had said "You already know that"?
qa.a: Yamini might feel brushed off, since the question was a way of seeking warmth, not just information.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler asking what-that with a rising tone and a point, a question that is as much social as informational.

passage:
“Look who's here, Charu!” said Rekha as Nani came through the gate.
Charu squealed, bounced on Rekha's hip and stretched both arms out. “Na-na!”
Nani laughed and took her.
At the wedding that evening, Rekha's cousin from Pune bent close. “Hello, Charu! Remember me?”
Charu stared at him, very still, then turned her face into Rekha's shoulder.
“She doesn't remember me?” he said.
“She was a tiny baby last time,” said Rekha.

qa.q: What did Charu say when she saw Nani?
qa.a: Charu said "Na-na!"

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she saw Nani, and how was that different with the cousin?
qa.a: With Nani she was delighted and eager, shown by her squeal and outstretched arms; with the cousin she stared and turned away because he felt like a stranger and she was unsure.

qa.q: How could the cousin help Charu get to know him?
qa.a: He could give her time and distance, talk with Rekha nearby, and let Charu look at him before expecting a greeting.

qa.q: How did Rekha's cousin feel when Charu turned away?
qa.a: He seemed a little hurt and surprised that she did not remember him.

grounding: It shows a toddler recognising a familiar person with a squeal and reaching, and staring and turning away from someone who feels like a stranger.
